description.summary: A mythical winged horse of East Asian tradition — Korean cheollima, Chinese qianlima — said to gallop one thousand li in a single day. Long used as a metaphor for exceptional talent in classical Chinese and Korean literature, and adopted in the 20th century as a state symbol in North Korea.
description.full: The cheollima (Korean 천리마, Hanja 千里馬; Chinese qiānlǐmǎ; Japanese senrima) is a mythical winged horse of East Asian tradition. The name literally means 'thousand-li horse' — a li being a Chinese unit of distance of about 0.5 km (modern) or roughly 0.4 km in classical use — and the creature is said to be capable of travelling one thousand li (approximately 400 km) in a single day, far beyond the reach of any ordinary horse, and to be too swift and excellent to be ridden by any mortal. The image originates in classical Chinese literature: it is associated with the legendary horse-judge Bo Le (伯樂), and with the proverb 'a thousand-li horse is common, but Bo Le is rare', meaning that exceptional talent goes unrecognised without a discerning patron. In Korea the figure was absorbed into Goryeo and Joseon literature and folklore, and acquired an additional life in the 20th century when the Workers' Party of Korea launched the Chollima Movement in late 1956 / early 1957 — a mass mobilisation campaign in the wake of the Korean War, modelled in part on the Chinese Great Leap Forward — and erected the 46-metre bronze Chollima Statue in Pyongyang in 1961. The cheollima is also the nickname of the North Korean men's national football team and lends its name to a 21st-century North Korean dissident movement (Cheollima Civil Defense / Free Joseon).

etymology.origin: Sino-Korean compound 千 (cheon, 'thousand') + 里 (ri/li, the East Asian unit of distance) + 馬 (ma, 'horse').
etymology.meaning: 'Thousand-li horse' — a horse capable of running one thousand li in a day.
etymology.first_use: The Chinese qianlima motif is attested in classical Chinese texts of the late Warring States and Han periods (c. 3rd c. BCE – 1st c. CE); the Korean cheollima is current in Goryeo and Joseon literature.

related_phenomena.name: Pegasus
related_phenomena.description: Greek mythological winged horse, with which the cheollima is sometimes loosely compared

features.description: In most modern visual depictions (including the Pyongyang statue) the cheollima has wings
Often depicted in art with powerful, rearing pose suggesting boundless energy

physical.morphology: A horse of mythical excellence, generally winged in modern depictions; older Chinese sources do not invariably wing it.

abilities.ability: Travel one thousand li in a day
abilities.description: The defining ability: travel of about 400 km in a single day
In classical tradition the cheollima is so swift and excellent that no ordinary rider can master it

habitat_preference: open plains and skies of East Asian myth
patterns: Functions as a metaphor for exceptional talent in literary tradition
Often paired with the figure of Bo Le, the discerning judge of horses

range.description: Sino-Korean cultural sphere; with strong modern presence in the Korean peninsula, especially North Korea.

hotspots.notes: Erected on April 15, 1961 (Kim Il-sung's birthday) to commemorate the Chollima Movement.

first_recorded.source: Classical Chinese texts of the Warring States / Han periods reference qianlima as a motif.

origins.cultural_roots: Classical Chinese horse-culture and the literary motif of recognising hidden talent (Bo Le and the qianlima); transmitted into Korean literature through Sino-Korean classical education.
origins.earliest_accounts: Classical Chinese references to qianlima are attested in texts associated with the late Warring States and Han periods.
origins.folklore_connections: Linked across East Asia through Sino-Korean and Sino-Japanese literary networks; modern North Korean usage is a 20th-c. political reappropriation.

timeline.event: The qianlima motif is established in classical Chinese literature, often paired with the figure of Bo Le (Sun Yang)
Workers' Party of Korea launches the Chollima Movement at the December 1956 plenum
timeline.significance: State adoption of the cheollima as an emblem of post-war reconstruction

timeline.event: Unveiling of the 46-metre Chollima Statue on Mansu Hill, Pyongyang
timeline.significance: Physical monument to the Chollima Movement

timeline.event: Cheollima Civil Defense (later Free Joseon) is formed as a dissident movement assisting at-risk North Koreans abroad
timeline.significance: 21st-c. dissident appropriation of the cheollima symbol

history.modern_era: The cheollima is a continuing live symbol in North Korean state imagery (Chollima statue, Chollima football team) and a literary metaphor in South Korea and the wider Sino-Korean cultural sphere. Its dissident usage by Cheollima Civil Defense / Free Joseon since 2017 has added a new political layer.

photographic.name: Chollima Statue, Pyongyang
photographic.description: 46-metre bronze statue depicting a winged horse carrying a male worker (with the 'Red Letter' from the Workers' Party Central Committee) and a female peasant.
photographic.analysis: Major North Korean monumental artwork; the canonical modern visual representation of the cheollima.

skeptical.name: Documented mythological and political symbol
skeptical.description: Wyrdness records the cheollima as a documented mythological figure and modern political symbol; there is no cryptozoological or paranormal claim attached to it.

traditions: Korean classical and modern literary tradition
stories: Bo Le and the unrecognised qianlima

Modern educational fables about diligence and talent
folklore.beliefs: The cheollima is widely understood as a literary and political symbol rather than a literal animal; in DPRK official discourse it functions as an emblem of national speed and self-reliance.

literature: Classical Chinese references in Han Yu's 'Discourse on Horses' (馬說)
